edges.why: Multiplying polynomials is repeated application of the distributive property, so a student who has not named it treats FOIL as a memorized pattern and stalls on a binomial times a trinomial.
Factoring out a greatest common factor is the distributive property read right to left, and without that identification the two operations look like unrelated tricks.
The addition and multiplication properties of equality used to solve are the real-number properties applied to both sides, so the solving steps otherwise stay memorized moves with no justification.
'Every integer is a rational number' is the first subset relation a student meets, so the formal subset definition later reads as a generalization rather than as brand-new notation.
The cost and revenue applications ask for the value of a polynomial at a stated production level, which is substitution into an algebraic expression.
Deciding whether an ordered pair solves an equation is substituting the x- and y-values and evaluating both sides.
Evaluating f(x) at a number is exactly substituting that number for the variable, including the negative-value cases that produce the standard sign errors.
Evaluating (-b +/- sqrt(b^2-4ac))/(2a) demands squaring before multiplying and dividing the entire numerator by 2a; mis-ordering yields a wrong root, not merely a slower one.
A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) comes out wrong unless the parenthesis is evaluated first, then the exponent, then the multiplication by P.
The standard-deviation formula is a nested expression (square the deviations, sum, divide, then take the root) and order errors are the dominant failure in computing it by hand.
An interval such as (-4,-1) cannot be placed on a number line without knowing which of two negative numbers is smaller.
Solving an inequality means tracking which side is larger at every step, including the reversal when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative.
The median cannot be located until the data values are put in increasing order, which is the ordering skill practiced here on mixed fractions, decimals, and negatives.
The 'graph the solution' half of every problem in 2.4 is this skill: open versus closed endpoint and which direction to shade.
Writing an inequality or interval notation from a pictured solution set is reading a number-line graph backwards, so it is unreachable without having drawn them.
Domains are reported in interval notation such as (-inf,3) U (3,inf), which is first encountered here and is otherwise a second new idea on top of exclusion values.
Positioning endpoints and choosing the shading direction presupposes knowing the order relation between the two endpoint values.
The product, quotient, and power rules are only meaningful once a^n is understood as repeated multiplication of a specific base.
Plotting y = a^x means computing the exponential at several x-values, including the negative ones that produce the fractional left tail.
Evaluating log_2 8 without a calculator is answering '2 to what power gives 8', so fluency with powers of small bases is what makes the question answerable mentally.
Finding a compound amount is the calculator evaluation of (1 + i)^n practiced here, now with awkward decimal bases and large exponents.
The convention separating -2^4 from (-2)^4 is an order-of-operations rule, and it is the single most common error in evaluating powers.
Multiplying terms such as (3x^2)(4x^3) requires adding exponents, so the distribution cannot be carried out without the product rule.
Simplifying with integer exponents is these same product, quotient, and power rules extended to zero and negative exponents.
The logarithm properties are the exponent rules rewritten, so a student fluent with a^m * a^n = a^(m+n) sees why log(xy) = log x + log y instead of memorizing three unrelated formulas.
The rules are derived by writing out the repeated multiplication, which is only convincing to a student who already reads a^n that way.
Like terms are defined by matching variable powers and answers are requested in descending powers, both of which are the degree-and-coefficient vocabulary named here.
The search rule for factoring x^2 + bx + c is stated entirely in terms of the constant term and the middle coefficient, so a student who cannot name those parts cannot follow the method.
The quadratic formula cannot be applied without first writing the equation in standard form and reading off a, b, and c in the correct positions.
Classifying a function as linear or quadratic is a degree judgment, and separating both from exponential is noticing that the variable has moved into the exponent rather than the base.
Profit equals revenue minus cost is a subtraction of two polynomials, including distributing the minus sign across the cost expression.
Solving 5x + 3 - 2x = 12 starts by combining like terms on each side; without that the equation never reduces to the form ax = b.
Factoring cannot begin until every term is moved to one side and combined into a single standard-form quadratic.
Subtracting a polynomial is distributing -1 across a parenthesis, the distributive property in its most error-prone form.
Deciding which terms may be combined is exactly deciding which terms share a variable and degree.
Revenue and cost models are built by multiplying a per-unit price by a quantity expression before any subtraction happens.
Factoring x^2 + 7x + 12 is undoing the product (x+3)(x+4); both the search for the pair and the check of the answer are statements about how that product expands.
The ac and grouping methods rest on knowing how (ax+b)(cx+d) expands, since that is where the split of the middle term comes from.
Every step of the expansion is the distributive property, so naming it is what generalizes FOIL beyond two binomials.
Each partial product requires adding exponents on the variable factors.
The product is not finished until the like middle terms produced by the distribution are collected.
The translate-a-situation-into-an-expression step is identical; the only new demand is that the expression is then set equal to something and solved.
The fixed-cost-plus-unit-cost revenue and profit problems reappear in 3.1 written in function notation, so a student who met them as polynomials faces only the new notation.
Answering 'what is the cost of producing 300 units' is substituting into and evaluating the cost polynomial.
Forming profit from revenue and cost is a polynomial subtraction.
Building a revenue expression as price times quantity is a polynomial product.
'Factor completely' problems require the common monomial to come out first, otherwise the trinomial left behind is not one the leading-coefficient-1 method applies to.
Factoring by grouping is repeated GCF extraction: pull the common factor out of each pair, then out of the two resulting terms.
Nothing can be cancelled until numerator and denominator are written as products, and pulling out the common monomial factor is the first step in doing so.
Equations such as 4x^2 + 10x = 0 are solved entirely by GCF factoring followed by the zero-product property.
Pulling out a common factor is the distributive property run backwards, and the check is redistributing.
Choosing the greatest common power of the variable is comparing exponents and using the quotient rule to see what is left inside the parentheses.
Reducing (x^2+5x+6)/(x^2-9) is impossible until both the trinomial and the difference of squares are rewritten as products.
The ac and grouping method extends the same 'two numbers with a given product and a given sum' search to the case where a is not 1.
The zero-product property has nothing to be applied to until the quadratic has been written as a product of two binomials.
The excluded values of a rational function are the zeros of its denominator, which are found by factoring that denominator.
The factored answer is validated by expanding it, and the middle-term condition being searched for is a fact about that expansion.
The method is phrased in terms of the constant term and the middle coefficient of a degree-2 polynomial.
Rational expressions in 1.4 carry numerators and denominators with a leading coefficient other than 1, which must be factored before any cancelling is legal.
Equations such as 6x^2 + x - 12 = 0 can only be solved by factoring if the leading-coefficient-not-1 case is handled.
Meeting non-monic trinomials that resist every factor pair is what makes the quadratic formula a needed tool rather than an arbitrary formula to memorize.
Grouping is GCF extraction applied to each pair of terms, and any overall common factor must be removed before the ac search gives the right pair.
The product-and-sum search is the same one, so students who own the monic case only have to absorb the extra split-and-group step.
Every product or quotient must be reported in lowest terms, and the cancelling is the same common-factor cancellation now done across two fractions.
The standing instruction to assume the denominator is nonzero is the domain restriction of a rational function, met before the word domain is introduced.
A quotient like (6a-6)/(33a+132) cannot be reduced until the common monomial factor is pulled out of each part.
Quadratic numerators and denominators must be factored into binomials before any factor can be cancelled.
Reductions involving a leading coefficient other than 1 stall completely if only the monic factoring method is available.
The answer to every multiplication or division must be written in lowest terms, so reducing is the closing step of each problem.
Dividing (12a+48)/(4a-44) by (a^2-16)/(a^2-3a-88) only collapses if every quadratic is factored before the invert-and-multiply step.
rational exponents are defined precisely so the integer-exponent rules keep holding, so x^(1/2)·x^(3/2) cannot be simplified without the product rule for integer exponents.
the left half of the graph of y = a^x is the set of points a^(-n) = 1/a^n, so without negative exponents a student can plot only x >= 0.
converting log_5(1/125) = -3 into 5^(-3) = 1/125 is impossible without knowing that a negative exponent means a reciprocal.
log(xy) = log x + log y and log(x^n) = n log x are the product and power rules read backwards, and students who never saw exponent rules as one system memorize the log rules as four unrelated facts.
solving 3^(...) = 81 'without using logarithms' means rewriting 81 as 3^4 and equating exponents, which cannot be done without fluency in rewriting numbers as powers of a common base.
the product, quotient and power rules for positive integer exponents are exactly the rules being extended to zero and negative exponents; without them there is nothing to extend.
knowing concretely that 2^5 = 32 is what makes 2^(-5) = 1/32 read as a definition that preserves the pattern instead of an arbitrary rule.
cancelling common factors to reduce x^5/x^2 is the quotient rule performed by hand, and meeting it first keeps 'subtract the exponents' from looking like a trick.
the exact solutions demanded by the quadratic formula problems require simplifying sqrt(b^2 - 4ac) by pulling perfect-square factors out of the radical.
recovering a from f(x) = a^x given f(2) = 16 means taking a square root of both sides, and the general 'find the rule through this point' problem needs an nth root.
finding the rate from $7000 accumulating to $7564 in 8 years requires r = (A/P)^(1/8) - 1, an eighth root; no amount of arithmetic recovers r without rational exponents.
a^(m/n) is defined so that the integer-exponent rules still apply, so simplifying (x^(2/3))^6 or x^(1/2)·x^(-3/2) is the integer rules applied to fractional exponents.
a student who can already see 32 as 2^5 and 81 as 3^4 reads 32^(1/5) and 81^(3/4) off directly instead of guessing.
solving A = P + Prt for t is the same isolation sequence performed with letters in place of numbers, so without the numerical version there is no procedure to generalize.
the zero-factor property converts a factored quadratic into two first-degree equations, x + 5 = 0 and x - 9 = 0, which must then be solved.
finding the intercepts of 2x + 3y = 24 without graphing is substituting y = 0 and solving the resulting first-degree equation 2x = 24, and again for x = 0.
solving -5p + 3 <= 23 is the identical isolation algorithm with one added sign rule; a student who cannot isolate p in an equation cannot isolate it in an inequality.
once both sides are written to a common base the problem collapses to a first-degree equation in the exponent, which is where the fractional answers like -4/3 come from.
an equation with terms on both sides cannot be reduced to ax = b without collapsing 3x + 2 - 5x into -2x + 2, which is adding and subtracting polynomials.
clearing the parentheses in 4(2x - 3) = 5x + 1 is an application of the distributive property, and students who cannot name it distribute over only the first term.
isolating the variable is undoing the order of operations in reverse, so a student who cannot state the order in which an expression was built cannot choose which step to undo first.
the check that every one of these problems demands is substituting the candidate back and evaluating the expression on each side.
ln(7x + 10) - ln x = ln 8 becomes (7x + 10)/x = 8, a rational equation whose denominator must be cleared before x can be isolated.
converting a Fahrenheit reading to Celsius means undoing the fractional coefficient in F = (9/5)C + 32, and students who have not cleared fractions in an equation stall at that step.
point-slope form with a fractional slope, y + 9 = (2/3)(x - 7), must have the fraction distributed and cleared before it can be reported in slope-intercept form.
after multiplying through by the LCD what remains is an ordinary first-degree equation, so this objective is one extra opening move on top of that one.
multiplying each term by the LCD and cancelling is exactly multiplication of rational expressions, so a student fluent there sees why the denominators vanish rather than erasing them by rote.
reading the slope and y-intercept off 2x = 3y + 9 requires first solving the equation for y, which is solving for a specified variable.
the conversion problems give one temperature formula and ask for the other unit, which is literally solving F = (9/5)C + 32 for C.
finding an interest rate means solving A = P(1 + r)^n for r, i.e. undoing the operations wrapped around r in a formula full of other letters.
present value is the compound-amount formula solved for P, and a student who cannot make that rearrangement has to memorize it as a second unrelated formula.
the sinking-fund payment formula is the future-value-of-an-annuity formula solved for R, so the two collapse into one idea only for students who can rearrange a formula.
the moves are identical - add the same thing to both sides, divide both sides by the coefficient - only with a letter rather than a number as the coefficient.
evaluating expressions in several letters builds the habit of treating a letter as a stand-in for a number, which is what allows P and r to be handled as constants while t is isolated.
making a prediction from a linear model is substituting into, or solving, the model equation, which is exactly the federal-debt and health-expenditure problems in a new setting.
writing the cost, revenue and profit rules for the pretzel factory is the same word-to-expression translation, now dressed in function notation.
every one of these problems ends with an equation such as 0.111x + 1.514 = 4 that has to be solved for x.
the other half of each problem is the reverse direction, substituting x = 15 into the model and evaluating the expression.
the translation from a described situation to a symbolic expression is first practiced on polynomial applications, and without it students can solve the equation but cannot write it down.

both methods start by forcing the equation into standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, and a student who has factored first knows when to reach for the formula instead of hunting for factors that do not exist.
2 ln(x - 7) = ln(x + 33) + ln 2 becomes (x - 7)^2 = 2(x + 33), a quadratic that must be solved by factoring and one of whose roots must then be rejected as extraneous.
equations like c^2 + 2c = 0 are solved only by pulling out the common factor c to get c(c + 2) = 0.
the zero-factor property applies to a product, so t^2 - 13t - 90 = 0 cannot be started until the trinomial is written as (t + 5)(t - 18).
the equations with a leading coefficient other than 1, such as 4x^2 + 4x - 3 = 0, are unreachable without the harder factoring technique.
setting each factor equal to zero produces first-degree equations like 2x - 3 = 0 that still have to be solved.
the exact answers these problems demand require simplifying the radical sqrt(b^2 - 4ac), for instance turning sqrt(72) into 6*sqrt(2).
the fraction bar spans the entire numerator, so a student without a firm grip on order of operations divides only the radical by 2a and gets a wrong root every time.
having solved by factoring first makes the formula a fallback for equations that will not factor rather than a black box replacing everything learned.
computing b^2 when b is negative is the classic sign error here, and it is the (-5)^2 versus -5^2 distinction from evaluating exponential expressions.
having produced solution sets like [4, infinity) by solving makes reading one off a number-line graph the inverse of a move the student has already made.
the domain of f(x) = 4/sqrt(23 - x) is found by solving the inequality 23 - x > 0, so without inequality solving every radical or even-root domain problem is out of reach.

answering 'the first full year in which the delinquency rate fell below 2.5%' means deciding which side of the crossing point satisfies the condition, which is reading a solution set rather than a single root.
solving 9x + 8 <= 44 is the same isolation algorithm as solving 9x + 8 = 44, with one extra rule about multiplying by a negative.
knowing what -4k <= -16 asserts about the order of two real numbers is what makes the direction reversal on dividing by -4 a consequence rather than a memorized quirk.
half of this objective is the words 'and graph the solutions', which is drawing an interval such as [4, infinity) on a number line.
every domain answer in 3.1 must be typed in interval notation, for example (-infinity, 23], so a student who cannot write an interval cannot report a domain at all.
reading a graphed solution set back into symbols requires already knowing what the bracket, parenthesis and arrow on a number line mean.
choosing between x < 3 and x > 3 for a shaded ray depends on knowing which direction on the line is 'less than', which is where real numbers were first ordered.
solving inequalities is where the bracket-versus-parenthesis convention is used for the first time, so describing a graph afterwards is recognition rather than a new convention.
plotting a point of a solution table is the same act as locating a point by the signs of its coordinates, so quadrant work removes the sign-placement errors that ruin a first graph
the slope formula assumes the student can read which number in (x1,y1) is the horizontal one, a habit first drilled by naming quadrants from ordered pairs
graphing intervals on a number line is the one-dimensional version of locating a value on an axis, and the coordinate plane is just two of those axes crossed
the quadrant of a point is decided entirely by whether each coordinate is greater or less than zero
graphing an equation means producing and plotting ordered pairs that satisfy it, so a student who cannot test a pair cannot generate the table
an intercept is the special solution pair with a zero coordinate, so seeing (7,15) tested against 11x-y-62=0 is what makes 'substitute 0 and solve' feel like finding a point rather than a ritual
checking that a pair satisfies an equation is function evaluation before the notation exists: input goes in, the arithmetic is done, the output is compared
deciding whether (7,15) satisfies 11x-y-62=0 is exactly evaluating an algebraic expression at given values of the variables
the substituted expression contains a product, a subtraction, and negative numbers, which is evaluated wrongly without order-of-operations discipline
the intercept method is a shortcut on the plot-several-points method, and students who never plotted a table treat 'two points determine the line' as an unmotivated rule
an exponential graph is drawn by evaluating the rule at a few x-values and plotting the resulting pairs, the identical procedure learned here on linear equations
every point plotted must be verified as a solution of the equation, otherwise the student plots arbitrary pairs
equations arrive as 5y+15x=25 and must be solved for y before a table of values can be built, which is solving a formula for a specified variable
each table entry has to be placed correctly in the plane, and sign errors in placement come from never having practised locating points by quadrant
seeing on a picture that intercepts are the crossings of the axes is what tells the student why the algebraic procedure sets a coordinate to zero
labelling intercepts on a sketched line presumes the student recognises what an intercept looks like on a drawn graph
reading a value off a supplied graph, as in the revenue-cost and share-price problems here, is the only earlier practice the course gives before students must extract counts from a supplied histogram
reporting an intercept as an ordered pair requires already reading positions in the plane as (x,y) pairs
graphing a line by intercepts is impossible without first computing the two intercepts from the equation
b in y=mx+b is meaningless unless the student already knows the y-intercept is the value of y when x is zero
describing an exponential graph starts by finding the second coordinate at first coordinate 0, which is a y-intercept computed from the rule
setting x=0 and solving produces a solution pair, so the substitution habit has to already read as 'making a point on the graph'
after substituting y=0 into 2x+3y=24 the remaining step is solving a first-degree equation for x
without the graphical picture the procedure is two unmotivated substitutions and students routinely report the intercepts with the coordinates swapped
comparing slopes for parallelism is empty unless slope is already a computed number with a meaning rather than a letter in a form
when the line is specified by two points the first step is literally the two-point slope formula
a linear model built from two data points is the slope of those two points used as a rate of change
classifying a table as linear is checking that the slope between successive pairs is constant, so the two-point slope computation is the test being run
the formula operates on two ordered pairs, and students who have not practised reading (x,y) pairs mix the coordinates and compute the reciprocal slope
the numerator and denominator are differences of signed numbers, as in -2-(-7), which is where most slope errors actually occur
extracting m and b from 3x-y=2 means recognising the target template y=mx+b, which is exactly what building the equation from m and b installs
every 'satisfying given conditions' answer must be delivered in slope-intercept form, so the form has to be available first
C=(5/9)(F-32) is a line with slope 5/9 and intercept -160/9, and students who cannot see it as such treat the conversion as a memorised recipe
the b that gets written into y=mx+b is the y-intercept, a quantity that has to already mean 'the y-value where x is zero'
writing m into the equation without having computed a slope from points leaves m as a symbol with no rate-of-change meaning
the parallel/perpendicular test compares the slopes of two lines given as equations like 4x+3y=4, which must first be converted to slope-intercept form
reading the slope of a fitted CPI line as 'index points per year' is the same interpretation practised on contextual equations such as y=5.2x+52
interpreting g(x)=587x+8851 as GDP growing 587 billion per year is the slope-and-intercept reading transferred to function notation
2x=3y+9 has to be solved for y before m and b are visible, which is solving an equation for a specified variable
the student is solving toward a template, and without having built y=mx+b themselves they do not know what shape to stop at
the two points being plotted are the intercepts, which must be computed from the equation first
the answer must be a sketch with intercepts labelled, which presumes recognising intercepts on a drawn graph
without the general plot-a-table method the intercept shortcut looks like a different technique instead of a faster choice of two points
both lines arrive as 6x-15y=7 style equations and the test cannot begin until each is converted to slope-intercept form
the negative-reciprocal condition is arbitrary symbol-matching unless slope is already understood as rise over run
making a prediction requires first producing the equation of the line through the two given data points, which is this objective applied to data
the Fahrenheit-Celsius relation is the line through (32,0) and (212,100), so deriving it rather than receiving it is what makes the formula checkable
'find the rule f(x)=a^x given f(2)=16' is the same workflow of pinning down a function's parameters from stated conditions, one family up
when the condition is 'through (5,2) and (3,5)' the slope must be computed from the two points before anything else
the required answer form is slope-intercept, so the student must already be able to assemble y=mx+b from a slope and an intercept
after substituting the given point, b is found by solving a first-degree equation, and students who are shaky there abandon the substitution step
converting in the other direction means solving C=(5/9)(F-32) for F, a formula rearrangement for a specified variable
the 5/9 and 9/5 coefficients mean every step is an equation involving fractions, and students who cannot clear them stall on the arithmetic rather than the modelling
recognising the conversion formula as a line with a slope and an intercept turns two memorised recipes into one relationship read in two directions
applications like the GDP function are the same act of substituting a coded year into a linear rule and reporting the predicted quantity, now dressed in function notation
exponential applications are the same predict-from-a-fitted-rule task with a multiplicative rather than additive rate, and the contrast is invisible to a student who never made a linear prediction

simple interest adds Pr dollars every year, so it is a line in t, and the linear-model reading is what later makes the break to compounding legible as a change of growth type rather than a new formula to memorise
the rate of change in the model is the slope between the two given data points
the model is the equation of the line through two given points, produced exactly as in that objective
the prediction step is substituting a coded x into the model, which is the ordered-pair substitution done without the checking
the answer usually has to be stated as a rate in context, which requires reading m as units per unit rather than as a number
building a profit function from a fixed cost, a unit cost, and a price is symbolic function construction, not numerical evaluation
reading f(2)=16 as a constraint on the unknown base a requires treating the argument of f as a symbol rather than as a number to be plugged in
f(a+2) is the algebraic expression x^2-1 evaluated at a symbolic value, which is the substitution skill itself
evaluating f(x)=x^2-1 at x+h forces the expansion of (x+h)^2, and without polynomial multiplication the student writes x^2+h^2
the expanded result must be collected into a simplified polynomial before it is recognisable as an answer
every function application here is answered by evaluating the given rule at a stated input
the points plotted for an exponential graph are obtained by evaluating the function at chosen x-values
answering 'how much natural gas in 2020' is evaluating f(t) at the coded t and nothing else
a logistic value is obtained by evaluating a nested fractional-exponential rule at a given input, where mis-sequenced substitution is the dominant error
f(3) is the expression 18x^2+2x evaluated at 3, so function notation adds a name but no new operation
evaluating 18x^2+2x at a negative input goes wrong without knowing that the square is applied before the coefficient
testing whether (7,15) solves an equation already pairs an input with its output, so f(x) names a process the student has performed
a candidate solution of a logarithmic equation must be discarded when it makes the argument nonpositive, which is the reject-inputs-outside-the-domain move learned here
